stem: A 28-year-old man arrives by ambulance following a motorcycle collision. He has a pelvic fracture and has been unable to urinate since the accident. Blood is seen at the tip of his penis, the lower abdomen is dull and tender above the pubis, and on rectal examination the prostate feels higher than normal. His blood pressure is stable.
oneliner: 28M + motorcycle crash, pelvic fracture + cannot void + blood at the meatus + prostate felt high → next step?

whyNot.A: Passing a tube **blindly through a possibly torn urethra** (meatal blood, high prostate) can worsen the tear
whyNot.B: Images the **kidneys and ureters**; the signs here (meatal blood, cannot void, high prostate) point to the **urethra**
whyNot.D: A scope is more invasive and is not the first look when **blood at the meatus** suggests a urethral tear
whyNot.E: Shows the kidneys and a full bladder, but the **urethra is the suspected injury**, not the upper tract

why: **Blood at the meatus, pelvic fracture, inability to void and a high-riding prostate** = posterior (membranous) urethral injury. A **retrograde urethrogram** shows the tear before anything is passed, because a blind catheter can convert a partial tear into a complete one.

idea.rule: If the urethra may be injured, image it before anything is passed through it.
also: Pelvic fracture tears the membranous urethra; a straddle injury tears the bulbar urethra
A perineal butterfly-pattern hematoma also points to urethral injury
If the urethrogram is normal, a Foley catheter can then be placed
If the urethra is torn, urine is drained with a suprapubic catheter

stem: A 22-year-old woman collapses near the end of a marathon after drinking large amounts of water at every aid station. Her weight is 3 kg above her weight at the start. She is semicomatose, and a generalized seizure occurred a few minutes ago. Her symptoms developed over a few hours. Serum sodium is 116 mEq/L.
oneliner: 22F + marathon + drank heavily, 3 kg heavier + semicomatose, seizure over hours + Na 116 → treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

whyNot.B: Isotonic saline adds little sodium relative to the **water she has already taken in** (3 kg gain) and is too weak for **a seizure at 116**
whyNot.C: Too slow: she is **seizing and obtunded** and needs sodium raised promptly
whyNot.D: A vasopressin antagonist acts too slowly and unpredictably for **seizure and coma**, and is not used for emergency correction
whyNot.E: Desmopressin **retains water**; she already has excess water (3 kg weight gain)

why: **Hyponatremia that developed over hours, with seizure and coma**, from water excess is a brain-swelling emergency. **3% saline** raises serum sodium by a few mEq/L quickly enough to relieve cerebral edema; when hyponatremia is chronic or of unknown duration, the total rise is kept to about **8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours** to avoid osmotic demyelination.

idea.rule: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia gets hypertonic saline, but the sodium must rise slowly after the first correction.
also: Chronic hyponatremia corrected too fast risks central pontine myelinolysis
If sodium overshoots, desmopressin with free water can bring it back down
Mild SIADH: fluid restriction, salt tablets or a vasopressin antagonist
Exercise-associated hyponatremia is water intake plus nonosmotic ADH release

stem: A 38-year-old woman, gravida 4 para 4, has had 6 months of small-volume urine leakage when she coughs, sneezes or lifts her children. She has no sudden urges and no trouble starting her stream. External genital examination is normal, and leakage is seen when she bears down. After voiding, a bladder scan shows a small residual volume. Urinalysis is normal.
oneliner: 38F + G4P4 + leaks with cough, sneeze, lifting + no urgency + small residual + leak on bearing down → first treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

whyNot.A: An antimuscarinic for **urgency and detrusor overactivity**; she has **no urgency**
whyNot.B: Raises detrusor contraction for **retention**; her **residual volume is small**
whyNot.C: For **overflow with a large residual**; hers is small
whyNot.D: An alpha-1 blocker for **outlet obstruction**; she has **no hesitancy or retention**

why: **Leakage only with cough, sneeze or bearing down, no urgency, small residual** = stress incontinence from urethral hypermobility after multiple vaginal deliveries. First-line treatment is **pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises**, which strengthen the levator ani.

idea.rule: Match the incontinence type to the treatment: stress needs a stronger floor, urge needs an antimuscarinic, overflow needs the outlet relieved.
also: Urge incontinence (detrusor overactivity): oxybutynin or other antimuscarinics
Overflow from an atonic bladder: bethanechol or catheterization
Overflow from BPH: tamsulosin or finasteride
Refractory stress incontinence: pessary or a midurethral sling

stem: A 52-year-old man with recurrent gout passes a kidney stone. It is not visible on his plain abdominal x-ray. Under the microscope, the crystals are yellow-brown and rhomboid. His urine pH is 5.0 on every check, urinalysis shows no bacteria, and his serum calcium is normal. He asks what can prevent more stones.
oneliner: 52M + gout + stone not seen on plain film + rhomboid yellow-brown crystals + urine pH 5.0 + normal Ca → prevent recurrence?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate way to prevent further stones?

whyNot.A: Lowers urinary calcium for **calcium stones**; his stone was **not visible on x-ray**, so it is not calcium
whyNot.C: **Acidifies** the urine, but his urine is **already acidic at 5.0**
whyNot.D: A urease inhibitor for **infection stones**; his urine shows **no bacteria**
whyNot.E: Not advised even for calcium stones (it raises oxalate absorption); his stone was **not visible on x-ray** and his **calcium is normal**

why: **Gout, a stone invisible on plain film, rhomboid yellow-brown crystals and a persistently acid urine** = uric acid stone. Uric acid is poorly soluble at low pH, so **potassium citrate** raises urine pH toward 6.5 and can even dissolve stones; allopurinol is added if urinary uric acid stays high.

idea.rule: Uric acid stones form in acid urine, so the treatment is alkalinization plus fluids.
also: Uric acid stones are radiolucent; calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque
Allopurinol lowers uric acid production when uric acid excretion is high
Tumor lysis syndrome and myeloproliferative disease raise uric acid load
Calcium oxalate stones are prevented with thiazides and citrate
